entry.title: Samiksha AI: Universal Review & comment Analyzer
entry.summary: Hey DEV Community! 👋 I recently participated in a hackathon and built Samiksha AI, a universal review and comment analyzer designed to turn messy customer feedback into structured business intelligence. Generic star ratings on e-commerce platforms don't give business owners the full picture. Rule-based sentiment tools often fail to catch sarcasm, background noise (like shipping complaints), or aspect-specific product feedback. I developed a python-based architecture that leverages: Google AI Studio (Gemini API): For advanced parsing, noise filtering, and Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis (ABSA). Streamlit Framework: To build an interactive, real-time executive report card dashboard. Plotly/Matplotlib: For rendering data distribution metrics dynamically. The code is structured with a clean separation between the data backend, core analytical engine, and user interface. You can check out the full open-source implementation here: 👉 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/TechSakhi/Samiksha-AI Building this pipeline gave me a deep appreciation for computational linguistics and structured datasets. Next, I plan to leverage these foundational concepts to explore building an AI agent focused on language learning systems! I would love to hear your thoughts, feedback, or suggestions on how to improve the architecture!

entry.summary: "Self-healing" is the most oversold phrase in data engineering right now. Most platforms wearing the label do two things: retry failed jobs and detect schema drift on supported connectors. Both are useful. Data teams lose a remarkable amount of time here. A Fivetran/Wakefield survey of 540+ data professionals found engineers spend around 44% of their time building and rebuilding pipelines. entry.title: Desenvolvendo uma Plataforma para Transformar a Comunicação Escolar
entry.summary: O Problema Durante pesquisas realizadas com estudantes, identificamos dificuldades relacionadas à comunicação entre alunos e professores, falta de canais adequados para feedback e problemas na divulgação de comunicados escolares. Muitos alunos relataram a necessidade de um ambiente digital mais organizado, participativo e acessível. Para resolver essa situação, desenvolvemos o Sistema de Avaliação Docente com Apoio Tecnológico, uma plataforma composta por site e aplicativo que centraliza informações acadêmicas, avaliações docentes, comunicados e interação entre a comunidade escolar. Stack Tecnológica Optamos por utilizar: HTML, CSS e JavaScript para o desenvolvimento da interface web. PHP para processamento das funcionalidades do sistema. MySQL para armazenamento seguro dos dados. Java e XML para o desenvolvimento do aplicativo Android. Android Studio e Visual Studio Code como ambientes de desenvolvimento. A escolha dessas tecnologias ocorreu devido à ampla documentação, facilidade de implementação e compatibilidade com projetos acadêmicos, permitindo construir uma solução robusta sem custos elevados. Desafios Encontrados Durante os testes, enfrentamos problemas na validação dos códigos enviados por e-mail e na sincronização das informações dos usuários. Após diversas análises e testes, conseguimos corrigir as inconsistências, garantindo segurança e confiabilidade durante o processo de login e recuperação de acesso. Esse desafio fortaleceu nossa capacidade de resolução de problemas e demonstrou a importância da realização de testes contínuos durante o desenvolvimento. Resultados Avaliação de professores com opção de anonimato. Envio de denúncias e sugestões. Consulta de agenda escolar. Visualização de notícias e eventos. Comunicação mais eficiente entre escola e alunos. Próximos Passos Pretendemos continuar aprimorando a plataforma, adicionando novas funcionalidades e melhorias na experiência do usuário.

entry.title: I'm a web dev who has never touched 3D. Here's my first creature.
entry.summary: New project, and I'm starting it the same way I start everything: slightly out of my depth, in public. I build web things. TypeScript, the browser, 2D canvas — that's home. The new project, NUMEN, is a god-game: you raise a creature and a little world grows around it. Which means for the first time I need 3D. And I have never made a single 3D model in my life. So this post isn't a tutorial. It's day one. The first thing I did was generate a creature with Meshy — text and an image in, a .glb model out. A cow, in three versions: gentle, neutral, and a darker one for when the creature gets raised badly. Twenty minutes ago they didn't exist; now they're sitting in my assets folder, rotating in a viewer, looking back at me. Here's the honest part, the thing I want to remember when this gets hard: getting a model out was easy. That's not the work. Two things hit me immediately: One model isn't a world. A cow that looks great alone means nothing if the temple, the trees, and the terrain all look like they came from different games. The actual skill I have to learn isn't "generate a creature" — it's keeping a whole world consistent. One style, every asset, or it's just a bag of mismatched outputs. So I'm not going to pretend I've "added 3D to my game." I made one creature. The renderer's still 2D. I don't know yet if I can pull the art of a whole world together as a solo dev who learned 3D yesterday. But there's a cow standing in 3D space that wasn't there this morning. For day one, that's enough to keep going. If you've made the jump from 2D/web into 3D: what's the thing you wish someone had told you on day one?
